newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German firms less confident, IFO says.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German firms less confident, IFO says.

text.p: Cracks appeared in a recent smooth upward trend in German business confidence on Monday after news that a key business climate index showed an unexpected dip in November.

The IFO index for West Germany, regarded as a crucial barometer of sentiment in industry, slipped to 96.9 in November from a revised 97.3 in October, interrupting a growth trend that included large jumps in the past four months.
The news sparked initial gains on German debt markets, which had expected another marginal rise in business confidence as the end of 1996, and expected economic improvement in 1997, approached.

However, the initial boost gave way after IFO, one of the country's most respected think-tanks, later said the Bundesbank was unlikely to ease its two main interest rates any further amid expected muted economic growth in Germany next year.
IFO also said the country's jobless rate, at a post-unification record, was likely to remain stubbornly high into 1997.

Economists downplayed the news, attributing the drop in business confidence to a temporary bout of pessimism after a recent spate of labour unrest, which was mainly sparked by employers' controversial efforts to implement new laws cutting sick pay by 20 percent.

"We think the upward trend in the IFO climate will go on in December," Commerzbank economist Christine Walter told Reuters Financial Television. "I think there is just some uncertainty in the market because of possible strikes and work stoppages."
Klaus Baader, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, London, said the IFO report came at a time of mixed signals on the economy, with orders rising but output not yet meeting expectations.
"In a few months output will follow orders," he predicted but conceded that recovery was proceeding more slowly than had been expected.
IFO predicted that the German economy would grow by 2.5 percent in 1997 as inflation remained moderate at 1.5 percent but said growth would be stymied by unemployment.
Jobless levels were likely to remain around their current highs of 4.1 million or 10.7 percent of the workforce on average throughout next year, the institute told a news conference in Munich.
At the same time, interest rates were likely to remain stable after the Bundesbank slashed its discount and Lombard rates to 2.5 percent and 4.5 percent last April.

"We do not think that the Bundesbank will cut its headline interest rates again," said IFO President Karl Heinrich Oppenlaender, adding that there was still a chance of some easing on the money market rate, or repo, now at three percent.
IFO also said the dollar, a key factor for exporters, would likely remain in a range of 1.50 to 1.55 marks next year, with a stronger tendency toward the upper end of the range.

It said increased revenue from the economic upturn and further efforts at consolidation would help Germany narrow its budget deficit to 3.2 percent of gross domestic product next year, just above the Maastricht Treaty reference value.
IFO's business indices, based on polls of key German industries, also showed declines in West German business conditions and expectations in November.
In the eastern states, however -- where recovery prospects are stronger -- the business climate index rose to 104.8 from a revised 102.5 in October.
